title: Polysubstance use: Diagnostic challenges, patterns of use and health

claims.statement: As summarized in two narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand and come from studies the reviews did not appraise, using more than one drug is common among people who use illegal drugs, how common depends on who was asked and how use was defined, and it makes the long-term effects of any one drug hard to study in people. Studies define it as using several drugs over a period (lifetime, or the past 1 to 12 months) or on the same occasion, the second being hard to capture in surveys and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples; the DSM-IV diagnosis of polysubstance dependence was dropped from DSM-5, and most population research records only how often each drug is used. Studies that group people by the drugs they use typically find a limited range (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate range (adding amphetamine-type drugs) and an extended range (adding prescription drugs used non-medically and other illegal drugs). Limited-range use was reported by 18% of 12- to 17-year-olds (ever) and by 34% of teenagers before 16, in two samples; extended-range use by 2% of 12- to 17-year-olds and 13.5% of 18- to 29-year-olds in Australian national samples, two different age groups that the review calls panel designs; and up to 75% of people at underground raves used several drugs, on average five at the last rave. Classes with a wide range of use reported more psychological distress, anxiety and depression in cross-sectional studies; several imaging studies and studies of self-control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, although the review's conclusion states cognitive deficits as clear; and the authors judged research on preventing and treating the use of several drugs underdeveloped (Connor et al., 2014). In the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006, the great majority of people who used it also used other drugs, most often alcohol, cannabis and stimulants: earlier studies found cannabis use in 90% to 100% of people who used ecstasy, and in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (1 to 9 pills in all) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions. Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore cannot separate ecstasy from the other drugs; in studies with comparison groups who used other drugs but not ecstasy (up to 234 people who used ecstasy), raised psychological problems went with drug use in general rather than with ecstasy, though those comparison groups mostly used drugs more moderately; earlier studies often did not record other drugs; and findings on whether cannabis explains, adds to or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions. The reviewers propose following young people at risk from before they start using drugs, for years, with drug histories recorded and psychological and cognitive tests repeated (Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann, 2006). How often people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis, and what that means for cocaine research, is in the answer on cocaine with alcohol and cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: As described, not pooled, no intervals. Connor et al. (2014): limited-range use 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime) and 34% of teenagers before 16; extended-range use 2% at 12–17 and 13.5% at 18–29 (Australian national samples of different age groups; 13.2% in the review's annotation of one source); up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs, on average five at the last rave; a sedative-and-alcohol class with last-year prevalence 1.3% among young Australian adults. Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann (2006): cannabis use in 90–100% of people who used ecstasy in earlier studies; in one survey all people new to ecstasy (1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions; comparison studies with up to 234 people who used ecstasy.
